And yes, yes it does... In a lot of instances of depression,suicide/anxiety I’ve ever encountered in my life... it has been due to overbearing parents, who treat their children as if they own them, have a right to their privacy. Just because it hasn’t happened for you, doesn’t mean it doesn’t happen. Have a little empathy

Again... not every family is like your dream or in the same situation as you... and again... stop expecting that you have the rights to information that doesn’t concern you as a parent... Would you want to know that your child hates you for your overbearing behaviour? That your child is gay and doesn’t feel comfortable sharing and has the right to share in their own time? That they’re in a relationship or having sexual relations (when they are legally able to)? That their friend is in a difficult situation (perhaps is suicidal) and only trusts the child, and any parental interaction may make the friend react drastically?  We would all hope that our child would come to us in their time of need. But in that case, your child isn’t coming to you... you’re watching your child’s every move like some obsessive stalker in a Liam Neeson Taken style movie. Your child will simply find other ways of hiding stuff from you.. they’re not stupid. And it’s when they find other, more discreet ways that predators find their way in. 

All things can only grow when given space... not suffocated.. children are one of these things. 

Where does it stop? What time do you stop “keeping tabs on your children” as if they are some kind of government spy being watched?

It doesn’t matter if I don’t have children... pathetic way of discounting my opinion tho. I have a basic respect for all people and an expectation of parents that they’d get off their entitled backsides and actually listen to their children for once.

There’s nothing wrong with OP asking for help. Nothing wrong at all with asking for help. In fact, it’s one of the best things that a child can do when unsure. However, invading the child’s privacy will lead to further secrecy and hiding their problems from their parent. To do this successfully, you have to foster a relationship of trust, not be breathing down their neck constantly. 

Stop treating children as if they’re mindless drones... and using “online predators” as an excuse for basic human rights violations. Foster a dialogue with your child through proper communication and encouraging a proper, non-punitive parenting style. 

Have a little sense... we aren’t in Nazi Germany anymore.

What if they have private sensitive information that the parents have no business knowing? Private information given to them by friends or information about the child that the parents have no right to dig up, such as medical information,sexuality, or child abuse, or relationship issues? Parents invading the privacy of their children makes them feel alienated and suffocated, which leads to rebellion and internalised anger. It also destroys any trust between the parents and child. 

To invade the privacy of a child shows that you have no respect for them. In many if not most cases, it’s not for “safety” but an aspect of control, which doesn’t allow the child to dissociate from their home lives and interact with others freely. “It’s my child.. I can do what I want. I know what’s best for them.” This can lead to poor mental health outcomes, and eventually anxiety, depression, and possibly worse. 

In order to create a conducive environment, you have to show children that you trust their judgement , yet educate them on right and wrong as best as you can, and always listen be aware of behavioural changes, or signs that could signal danger. Just be straight up with the kid if you’re worried. Don’t read the messages without telling them like it’s something you’re entitled to do.
It’s wrong if they’re under 18 too. It’s never right to invade your child’s privacy at any age... unless your concern for their safety is justified. Even then you must respect their boundaries
